commit.message:
fix(flex): guard sum fast path with layout_covers_storage_once (#5634)

* fix(flex): guard sum fast path with layout_covers_storage_once

sum_f32 reduced the raw buffer whenever numel equalled the buffer length.
That is necessary but not sufficient for a view to be a bijection onto
storage: a broadcast dim has stride 0, so the view reads some elements
twice and others never while the counts still match. An expanded [2,2]
view with strides [0,1] over a 4-element buffer summed to 6.0 instead of
2.0.

Use layout_covers_storage_once, which max/min already use. It verifies
the strides form a dense sequence covering storage exactly once, so
permuted and flipped tensors keep the fast path while broadcast,
overlapping, gapped and partial views fall back to strided iteration.

Fixes #5600

* test(flex): cover overlapping unfold in sum regression tests

unfold(0, 3, 2) over six elements yields two overlapping windows whose
element count equals the buffer length, so it hit the same fast path as
the expanded view: index 2 is read twice and index 5 never, summing the
raw buffer to 15.0 instead of 12.0.

fix(store): harden and restructure the PyTorch reader (#5593)

* fix(store): harden and restructure the PyTorch reader

Rework the pickle parser around a single tensor-building path shared by
every container format, and make each container's storage lookup explicit.

- Support pickle protocols 0 through 5 (protocol 4 checkpoints failed on FRAME)
- Resolve ZIP entries under the directory holding data.pkl, so version and
  byteorder are actually read and storages need no per-tensor archive scan
- Read the real pre-0.1.10 TAR layout (tensors table, persistent id strings)
  and regenerate the TAR fixtures in that layout
- Refuse broadcast views above 1 GiB instead of materializing them
- Keep unknown Python objects opaque instead of failing the load; only
  unknown torch._utils._rebuild* calls remain an error
- Fix _rebuild_from_type_v2 and _rebuild_parameter argument handling; add
  _rebuild_parameter_with_state and _rebuild_tensor_v3
- Bound allocations from untrusted lengths, use checked arithmetic in TAR
  parsing, verify legacy storage counts and reject truncated files at open
- Parse legacy files once instead of skipping and re-reading the main pickle
- Replace lazy_data with storage: one immutable source per container, no
  nested locks, ZIP archive opened once
- Decode tensor bytes directly instead of per-dtype element loops
- Make pickle_reader and storage private; re-export PickleError and OpCode

* refactor(store): tighten the PyTorch reader after review

- Carry the storage source on StorageRef so REDUCE dispatch and tensor
  construction no longer thread the persistent id resolver through
- Replace the opaque Reduce/Build variants with a single Opaque, and decide
  structurally (arguments holding a storage or tensor) rather than by name
  which uninterpreted calls are unsupported tensors
- Use burn-pack's MAX_TENSOR_SIZE as the one materialization ceiling instead
  of a separate broadcast-only constant
- Share key_string and non_negative between the pickle and TAR parsers; add
  tar_fields and read_tar_usize for the repeated TAR table reads
- Return TAR storage info from parse_tar_storages instead of downcasting the
  source back to TarSource
- Restore a match for OpCode::try_from
- Reserve read buffers up to a caller-supplied bound instead of growing from
  zero; compute ZIP data_size on demand from data entries only
- Make From<PickleError> uniform and move the NoDataSource hint into its
  Display text

* fix(store): close review findings in the PyTorch reader

- Clamp TAR table preallocation to the entry size; a count pickle of 2^40
  aborted the process instead of returning an error
- Reject LONG values whose 9th byte is sign fill but whose sign bit
  disagrees (2^63 truncated to i64::MIN)
- Track MARK as stack positions instead of a sentinel value, so a mark can
  no longer be wrapped, memoized or returned as an object
- Cap container nesting at 1000 levels; deeper pickles overflowed the stack
  during extraction and conversion
- Check BUILD objects and NEWOBJ_EX kwargs for tensor data, not just args
- Error on OrderedDict arguments that are not a list of pairs
- Reject untyped storages carrying view metadata
- Require the TAR storage-views list and the legacy protocol version 1001,
  as PyTorch does
- Model the legacy declare/finish protocol as a two-state enum
- Use checked arithmetic when slicing TAR storages
- Mark PytorchError, PickleError and OpCode non_exhaustive
- Correct doc claims about PyTorch versions, ZIP roots and metadata fields
- Add tests: archive/ and root-level ZIP layouts, _rebuild_from_type_v2,
  legacy element-count verification, bool normalization, TAR storage view
  fixture, legacy big-endian refusal, nesting and mark handling

* test(store): pin strided view layouts against an independent reference

Cover the layouts real checkpoints produce (channels_last, transposes, step
slices, overlapping windows, size-one dims with leftover strides, inner
expands, empty views at the end of storage) and non-contiguous views over
i16, u8 and f64 storages. Restore the non-integer stride rejection test.

* fix(store): address review of the PyTorch reader

- Charge memo lookups and DUP against a copied-bytes budget as well as a
  node budget, so a memoized large payload cannot be amplified
- Read only the bytes a tensor's view can touch from a storage, and cap
  data.pkl at MAX_METADATA_SIZE and text entries at 4 KiB, so a deflated
  entry cannot decompress past its archive size unchecked
- Refuse _rebuild_from_type_v2 state that holds tensors
- Decode protocol 0 UNICODE payloads as raw-unicode-escape
- Reject byteorder values other than little and big

* chore(store): drop the redundant burn-tensor dependency

The pytorch feature pulled burn-tensor in for one import of Bytes, which
burn-core already re-exports.

* Update Cargo.lock

* fix(store): check ZIP entry checksums and keep oversized ints opaque

Reading a ZIP entry through a bounded reader stops at its own limit, so the
CRC the zip crate validates at EOF never ran. Whole-entry reads now probe one
byte past the declared size, which reaches EOF and runs the check.

A Python long wider than i64 no longer fails the load: it becomes an opaque
object, so metadata such as a seed of 2**64 does not reject the checkpoint.

* fix(store): bound storage reads and tighten legacy header checks

A tensor now reads only the window its view can touch. Bytes before the
window are decompressed and dropped rather than held, so a tiny tensor at a
large offset no longer retains the whole prefix.

A legacy storage view's declared size bounds what a tensor may reach, instead
of the root storage's size. Parameter state holding a tensor is refused rather
than dropped along with the tensor.

The legacy magic number is recognized in every protocol's encoding, and the
first pickle is consumed as a pickle rather than skipped by a fixed offset, so
files written at protocols other than 2 are no longer misread as plain
pickles. A sys_info without a little_endian bool is an error instead of an
assumed little-endian file.

* test(store): use a test string the typo checker accepts

The raw-unicode-escape test spelled its sample text with a Latin-1 e-acute,
leaving "caf" as a bare token that the typos check reads as a misspelling of
"calf". The string is incidental to what the test covers, so it now uses one
whose ASCII letters spell nothing.

commit.message:
perf(cubecl): walk elementwise kernels in operands' memory order (#5625)

* refactor(std): move the dimension-order helpers to burn-std

`dim_order`, `nested_dim_order` and `is_contiguous_order` answer a question
about a tensor's strides alone — which dimension is innermost, which next,
whether the layout is dense or merely nested — and nothing in them is about
fusion. They lived in `burn-cubecl-fusion`'s launch planner because that was
the first place to ask. The elementwise kernels in `burn-cubecl` are about to
ask the same question, and `burn-cubecl` cannot depend on the fusion crate.

Both crates already depend on `burn-std`, which is where `is_dense` and
`is_contiguous` sit, so the helpers and their tests move there as
`burn_std::tensor::layout`. The fusion planner re-exports them from the same
path it always did; `strides_for` and `permuted_innermost_axis` stay, being
about the planner's own reference layout.

No behaviour changes.

* perf(cubecl): walk the elementwise kernels in their operands' memory order

The elementwise kernels take every operand through a linear view that walks
the logical dimension order, and allocate their output contiguous in that
order. A convolution hands its consumer a channels-last tensor presented in
NCHW, so any elementwise operation that does not fuse — a gradient's
`grad * x` in a backward pass, a scalar multiply, an activation — walked it
strided, and because the logical last dimension is not the contiguous one it
could not vectorize either. Now that the fusion planner keeps such tensors
channels-last, every unfused consumer paid this on every activation.

An elementwise operation does not care what a dimension means, only that its
operands are walked in step. So `in_memory_order` hands the operands to the
kernel permuted into the order the bulk of them occupy memory in — a
byte-weighted vote among the operands of the output's shape, ties to the
logical order, padding under a dimension tolerated — and permutes the result
back. The output is then allocated dense in that order, an operand already in
it is walked linearly and vectorized, one that disagrees is walked strided
exactly as before. A permute is a change of metadata, so no data moves, and a
quantized operand is left alone.

Applied to the float and numeric binary, scalar and unary launchers.

Measured on CUDA (one L4), same session, warm, first pass discarded, median
of twenty, on a convolutional classifier whose activations are channels-last:
a training step went from 418.7 ms to 364.2 ms, the backward within it from
225.7 ms to 181.5 ms, and the cost of running the forward under autodiff from
31.9 ms to 19.4 ms. The forward pass itself, which is fused end to end and
never reaches these kernels, was unchanged (166.7 ms against 166.0 ms).

Six tests compare each kernel on a channels-last operand against the same
kernel on a contiguous copy, on the plain backend and under fusion. The whole
tensor target on metal without fusion is unchanged: 1625 passed, and its one
failure, `int::ops::powi::should_support_powi_broadcast`, fails identically
on main.

* Preserve singleton vectorization and resolve memory-order ties

ask the same question, and `burn-cubecl` cannot depend on the fusion crate.

path it always did; `strides_for` and `permuted_innermost_axis` stay, being

The elementwise kernels take every operand through a linear view that walks
the logical dimension order, and allocate their output contiguous in that
order. A convolution hands its consumer a channels-last tensor presented in
NCHW, so any elementwise operation that does not fuse — a gradient's

strided, and because the logical last dimension is not the contiguous one it
could not vectorize either. Now that the fusion planner keeps such tensors

byte-weighted vote among the operands of the output's shape, ties to the
logical order, padding under a dimension tolerated — and permutes the result

quantized operand is left alone.

tensor target on metal without fusion is unchanged: 1625 passed, and its one

on main.

refactor(dataset): back SqliteDataset with Turso instead of rusqlite (#5546)

* refactor(dataset): back SqliteDataset with Turso instead of rusqlite

Replace rusqlite, r2d2_sqlite and serde_rusqlite with the pure Rust Turso
engine. The public API is unchanged: SqliteDataset, SqliteDatasetStorage,
SqliteDatasetWriter and SqliteDatasetError keep their names, and database
files stay byte compatible in both directions.

The `sqlite` and `sqlite-bundled` features collapse into one, since a pure
Rust engine has no bundled-versus-system split. `sqlite-bundled` is kept as
an alias so existing dependents keep building.

`sqlite` also moves out of burn-dataset's default features. Turso is heavier
than rusqlite when enabled, and a pipeline built on CSV or in-memory sources
has no use for either: the default drops from 150 crates to 43. Depending on
`burn/dataset` alone no longer provides `SqliteDataset`, so `burn/sqlite` has
to be requested. Turso's own default features stay off, which is required
rather than merely lean: its `fts` feature pulls a tantivy release whose
`lz4_flex` requirement cannot be resolved. Note that this does not make the
build free of C: turso_core pulls simsimd, which compiles C unconditionally. Making the feature opt-in also
exposed `audio` relying on `sqlite` without declaring it.

Turso's API is async, but for a local database file every poll runs its IO
inline, so futures_lite::block_on drives it without a reactor. A connection
rejects concurrent use at runtime, so reads keep an r2d2 pool while the
writer serializes on a single connection behind a mutex.

Three engine differences needed handling:

- Turso is WAL-only and ignores `journal_mode = OFF`, so autocommit inserts
  pay a WAL commit per row. Inserts are batched into transactions instead,
  which leaves concurrent writes faster than before rather than slower.
- Closing a connection does not fold the WAL back into the database file, so
  set_completed checkpoints first. The pragma reports a refused checkpoint
  through a result row rather than an error, so the row is inspected: an
  unchecked Ok would publish a dataset missing almost all of its rows.
- Turso answers `max(row_id)` from the index only when the aggregate stands
  alone, so the row count no longer wraps it in `coalesce`. Wrapped, it
  degrades to a full table scan: 86ms versus 5ms to open a 560k row split.

Adds a serde row deserializer to replace serde_rusqlite, preserving the same
column-name-to-field mapping.

* Preserve serde row deserialization shapes

perf(autodiff): reduce a broadcast gradient over all dims at once (#5623)

* perf(autodiff): reduce a broadcast gradient over all its dimensions at once

`broadcast_shape` sums a gradient back down to the shape it was broadcast
from, and did so one dimension at a time: a parameter broadcast over batch
and space paid three reductions and two intermediates, the first of them
nearly the size of the gradient itself. In the backward pass of a
convolutional network with a normalization after every convolution, half of
all reductions were such chain links, each its own launch and almost all of
them under twenty microseconds.

`FloatTensorOps::float_sum_dims` reduces several dimensions in one call. Its
default is the old per-dimension fold, so every backend keeps working
unchanged. `broadcast_shape` calls it once, as does `Tensor::sum_dims`.
Fusion forwards it as a single operation, `NumericOperationIr::SumDims`, so
the reduction reaches the backend whole instead of as separate single-axis
operations that nothing could recombine; the router executes it the same way.

`burn-cubecl` folds the reduced dimensions into one axis by a stride change
where they sit next to each other in memory, and reduces once — for a
channels-last activation every non-channel dimension does. The folded axis
goes first and the kept dimensions after it, so the kept innermost dimension
stays innermost in memory: the reduction coalesces across it and writes its
output vectorized along it, rather than walking a strided last axis. Where the
reduced dimensions do not all sit together, the outermost is reduced first;
its output is contiguous, so the rest then fold, and no layout takes more
than two launches.

Measured on CUDA (one L4), same session, warm, first pass discarded, median
of twenty, on a convolutional classifier with channels-last activations: a
training step went from 369.7 ms to 362.0 ms; reduce launches per step fell
by 40% and the time spent in them by 30% (115 ms to 80 ms), most of which
had been overlapped with other work. The forward pass, which does not
reach this path, was unchanged.

Five tests compare `sum_dims` on channels-last and contiguous operands with
reducing one dimension at a time, on the plain backend and under fusion. On
metal: autodiff 564 passed, tensor 1630 passed with the one pre-existing
`int::ops::powi::should_support_powi_broadcast` failure unchanged.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5.1 <noreply@anthropic.com>
Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_01M5Stct4YPegPaTw8oxyZzd

* fix(cubecl): fold only the dimensions memory already holds together

The routine presented every reduced dimension first and folded the lot into
one axis. Where they do not all sit together in memory the fold fails, and the
fallback then reduced the outermost of them *under that presentation* — a view
whose innermost axis is the kept one, so consecutive output elements read
addresses a whole kept extent apart. A contiguous NCHW tensor reduced over
batch and space paid that on its largest launch: `sum_dims([0, 2, 3])` on a
[4, 48, 384, 384] tensor went from 10.9 ms on the tensor-op path to 40.4 ms,
and a broadcast gradient reduced back over batch and space from 15.1 to 44.7.

Each pass now takes the largest run of reduced dimensions that memory does hold
together, presents that run first and reduces it, and puts the output back in
logical order before the next pass. Channels-last still folds every non-channel
dimension into one launch, since all three are one run there. NCHW folds height
and width first, which leaves 192 elements rather than the 28 MB intermediate
both the previous shape and the tensor-op path wrote, and reduces batch after.
A layout that scatters the reduced dimensions takes no more launches than
reducing them one at a time would have, and every launch reduces a dense axis.

`reshape_action` cannot express the fold: it declines a merge on a permuted
view even when the dimensions being merged are densely nested. The run is
known to be dense by construction, so the folded axis takes the stride of the
innermost dimension in it directly.

Metal: the six `reduce_dims` cases pass, tensor 1625 passed with the one
pre-existing `powi_broadcast` failure, autodiff 564/0.

* fix: comment over missing handling for zero lenght dimension

Also added alloc::vec for no std build

* test: cover initially drop case

commit.message:
perf(cubecl): scatter-add runs one unit per value with atomic adds (#5621)

* perf(cubecl): scatter-add runs one unit per value with atomic adds

The scatter kernel ran one unit per output row and walked the scatter
axis serially. That leaves the device nearly idle whenever the values
far outnumber the output rows: a histogram of a million values into a
few thousand bins ran on a thousand units each looping over every value,
and cost the same whether the batch was 32 or 128.

For `Add`, on a type the device adds atomically, a second kernel now runs
one unit per value and applies each update with an atomic add. The
serial kernel stays for `Assign`, `Mul` and `Or`, whose order matters or
which have no atomic form, and for types without atomic support. On
floats the order the adds land in is not fixed, so a sum's rounding can
differ between runs where the serial kernel was deterministic.

A test scatters two thousand ones into eight slots so every slot is hit
hundreds of times and the counts must come out exact.

Measured on an L4 (CUDA), a 1-D convolution bank whose counting scatters
1.6 million values into 8,192 slots sixteen times a pass, same session,
medians of 20 with the first pass of each binary discarded: the training
step 95.9 -> 81.2 ms, repeated 81.5 ms (-15%). In isolation the two
scatters of one dilation went from 1.45 ms to about 0.3 ms.

* chore: remove comment

* Gate CPU

Feat/storage tiled carrier (#5631)

* update cubek

* chore: pin cubecl (metadata guards) and cubek (storage-tiled write, pack, selector)

* feat(cubecl): carry a storage-tiled tensor through burn, and read it only where it was packed for

A tensor packed into storage tiles (cubek's pack) now survives every
conversion: TensorHandle is built from the whole metadata, to_client keeps
it, and CubeFusionHandle carries the tiling beside its strides so the two
boundary conversions and its binding lose nothing. Burn's view of the
tensor is its logical shape (shape/rank fold the tiling), so the matmul
output is sized right; the eager matmul hands the binding to cubek, which
stages to the tiles, and the tuner keys on the storage and adds the tiled
cmma as the candidate for a packed operand.

Everything else reads rows: the layout rewrites (into_contiguous, reshape,
expand, unfold, slice, repeat_dim, q_reshape, the im2col views, reduce)
lay a packed tensor back in rows first through kernel::untile; a kernel
argument refuses one; a fused kernel refuses one at input registration,
and the fused matmul falls back to the eager path when an operand is
packed.

* chore: pin cubek at main 8c39f6d (#630 + #631) and cubecl at its 2f81491

commit.message:
perf(flex): write slice_assign in place when the destination is uniquely owned (#5603)

* perf(flex): write slice_assign in place when the destination is uniquely owned

slice_write_impl takes its destination by value and then shadows it with
`let mut tensor = tensor.to_contiguous();`. Because to_contiguous borrows,
its already-contiguous fast path returns self.clone(), and the shadowed
parameter is never moved, so it stays alive holding a second Arc handle.
Arc::strong_count was therefore 2 when storage_mut() reached Arc::make_mut,
and the copy-on-write check copied the whole destination on every call,
making slice_assign O(destination) regardless of ownership.

Add a consuming into_contiguous(self) whose fast path returns self instead
of a clone, and use it in slice_write_impl. to_contiguous now delegates to
it so the fast-path predicate has a single definition.

Fixes #5575.

* perf(flex): write uniquely-owned contiguous prefix views in place too

`into_contiguous`'s fast path requires the logical tensor to cover the whole
buffer, so a contiguous prefix view (`narrow(dim, 0, n)`) is copied even when
the caller owns it. That check exists for callers that read `storage()` by
length (#4855); `slice_write_impl` is not one of them, since every write it
does is computed from `dst_layout`, whose canonical strides and zero start
offset keep it inside the logical prefix.

Use the crate's usual in-place predicate here instead, matching `bool.rs` and
`unary_op_typed`. Uniqueness stays in it: a shared prefix view has to be
compacted, or `Arc::make_mut` would duplicate the parent's whole buffer rather
than just the view, and leave the result oversized for every later write.

Three tests, each pinning one conjunct. The last one matters most: before it,
dropping either `is_contiguous()` or `start_offset() == 0` left the whole suite
green, because nothing else hands `slice_assign` an offset or transposed
destination.

docs(flex): fix stale statements in burn-flex docs and comments (#5619)

* docs(flex): fix stale statements in burn-flex docs and comments

Every claim below was re-checked against the current source.

README:
- Integer matmul is a nested loop with a SIMD i32 dot product
  (`ops/matmul.rs`), not gemm; gemm has no integer kernels.
- Conv transpose is gemm + col2im (`ops/conv_transpose.rs`), and it is
  burn-ndarray that uses a direct scatter loop, so the table note had the
  two backends the wrong way round.
- Quantized layout ops are zero-copy only for per-tensor schemes; block
  schemes go through `block_safe_layout_op`, and `q_select` always
  materializes.

COMPARISON:
- ActivationOps: flex overrides every method except `log_softmax` and
  `softmin`; ndarray overrides `relu` only.
- interpolate: Lanczos3 is implemented, and ndarray also has
  nearest-exact.
- Q ordering/layout rows: same per-tensor vs block distinction as above.
- SIMD dispatch is `#[macerator::with_simd]`.
- Dependencies: 8 required (libm was missing) + 5 optional (`once_cell`,
  `portable-atomic`). gemm is pinned at 0.19, not 0.18.
- Codebase size: 44 files / ~34,200 lines, remeasured for both backends.
  Added the counting method so the numbers can be reproduced.
- Binary ops (f32) is ~1x, matching BENCHMARKS.md and the README; the
  2.4-3.9x figure predates ndarray gaining macerator SIMD for f32.

ARCHITECTURE:
- `checked_index` is a release-mode check, not a debug assertion.
- Integer ops widen to i64 before applying the op, so shifts mask the
  shift amount to 64 rather than to the operand's own width.

Source comments:
- `backend.rs`: `float_random`/`int_random` store the advanced RNG back
  into `SEED`, so draws after `seed()` stay deterministic.
- `activation.rs`: `ActivationOps::softmax` and `ModuleOps::layer_norm`
  hooks both exist and are wired up.

Fixes #5614

* docs(flex): address review on quant, interpolate, shift and f32 binary ops

Follow-up to the review on #5619. Each item re-checked against source.

COMPARISON:
- Quantization: `q_argmax`/`q_argmin` reduce over the i8 payload for
  every scheme (`ops/qtensor.rs`), so the per-tensor qualification only
  belongs on the layout ops, `q_select` and `q_gather`.
- interpolate: ndarray's `NearestExact` arm panics
  (`burn-ndarray/src/ops/module.rs`) and flex has no arm for it, so
  neither backend implements nearest-exact. Both cover the same four
  modes.
- ActivationOps: the overrides are fused, not single-pass. `softmax` is
  documented in `ops/activation.rs` as a three-pass row kernel.
- Binary ops (f32): keep the allocation advantage. `binary_op_typed`
  reuses a uniquely owned operand in place, so a chained expression
  avoids the output buffer even where the standalone benchmark ties.
  BENCHMARKS.md measures ~1-1.4x. README row updated to match.

ARCHITECTURE:
- Narrow the i64 widening note to the paths that actually widen. u64
  arithmetic, division and remainder take a dedicated u64 path in
  `ops/int.rs` because values above i64::MAX cannot round-trip.

Source comments:
- `ops/int.rs`: the shift comment claimed masking to the operand type
  width, which contradicts the widening. Corrected, and pinned by a test
  asserting that `1i32 << 33` yields 0 through the backend while a native
  `i32::wrapping_shl(33)` yields 2.

commit.message:
perf(fusion): settle only the unfusable head of a block (#5622)

When a dependent block is committed and no fuser has a fusion worth
executing, `Block::optimize` returned the whole block as unfused
operations. A block is a dependency chain, so everything after the
operation that closed the fusers ran one kernel each, although a fresh
fuser would have fused it: those operations only sat in that block
because they depend on its head. The common heads are a lone elementwise
op followed by a view of its own output, a convolution backward, or a
reduction — a single fused op scores zero — which is what a backward
pass is made of. On a convolutional network's training step the fusion
log showed 3,588 one-op segments per step and 3,238 elementwise ops
executing unfused, 2,504 of them in runs of two or more consecutive
fusable ops.

Now only the head is settled: the operations up to and including the one
that closed the last fuser, plus whatever follows that no fresh fuser
would start on (probed by feeding it to a clone of each pristine fuser).
The rest goes back to the search — as a hole re-optimized in the same
plan, or as the next segment — exactly as the tail of a block that did
have a fusion already did. The stream optimizer passes its pristine
fusers down for the probe, and each block records the registration index
at which every fuser closed.

The operation that closed the last fuser is settled with the head even
when a fresh fuser would start on it, so a block that closes on its
second operation keeps executing as one segment, as before. Leaving it
to the search would win a fusion in some cases at the price of more
segments; that is a separate decision, not taken here.

Three tests cover the behaviour (an unfusable head leaves its fusable
tail to the next search; the tail is fused as a hole when an independent
block follows; the closing op stays with the head) and one expectation
was updated: an in-block reorder is still refused, but the second op is
no longer dragged along unfused. In `Sync` mode the explorer folds the
leftover tail back into the plan unfused, so the gain is in lazy
execution.

Measured on an L4 (CUDA), a convolutional classifier training step at
batch 4, same session, medians of 20 with the first pass of each binary
discarded: 366.1 -> 320.0 ms and, repeated, 370.8 -> 324.8 ms (-12.5%);
the plain forward (178.8 vs 179.7 ms) and a 1-D convolution bank
(99.8 vs 99.9 ms) unchanged.

perf(fusion): let a padded tensor vote for the block's layout (#5620)

* perf(fusion): let a padded tensor vote for the block's layout

A fused block picks the dimension order of its output by a byte-weighted
vote among its inputs, so that a block fed a channels-last tensor iterates
channels-last and reads it linearly instead of strided. The vote asked each
input for its `dim_order`, which requires the tensor to fill its buffer
exactly. A tile-aligned or pitched allocator does not do that: it leaves a
gap under the innermost dimension, so 48 elements held innermost on a
64-element tile carry stride 64 where a dense tensor would carry 48.

Such a tensor is not dense, so it could not vote. With no voters the block
kept a contiguous reference, wrote its output vectorized and read its large
channels-last input one element at a time. Nothing failed; the layout
propagation simply never fired on a backend whose allocator pitches rows,
for every channel count that is not tile-aligned. A backend with dense
allocations took the fast path all along, which is why the gap only showed
up as a difference between backends.

`nested_dim_order` accepts a gap (padding) and still rejects an overlap,
and the vote uses it. That is enough because the vote only decides the
*order* the output is allocated in, and the output is allocated dense in
that order either way; a padded input whose strides then differ from the
reference is read through the strided path, since `SameAsRef` compares
strides exactly. `dim_order` is unchanged wherever a buffer is
reinterpreted as a flat run of elements.

Measured on CUDA (one L4), warm, median of ten: an elementwise
normalization plus activation over a channels-last view of a
[4, 48, 384, 384] tensor went from 6.28x the contiguous case to 1.10x;
a convolutional encoder pass 1.58x faster; a full forward pass 1.6x
faster; a training step 1.11x faster.

Six unit tests cover the new order. burn-backend-tests with
--features cuda,fusion is green on every target except two in-place
alias-count tests under f16 that behave identically with and without this
change: `reduce_fusion_elemwise_output_writes_inplace` fails
deterministically when run alone on main (its f16 input arrives
row-pitched and the alias gate refuses it; in a suite it passes only when a
concurrent test bumps the global counter inside the window), and
`broadcast_elemwise_writes_inplace_and_computes_correctly` is
order-dependent for the same reason.

* Fix docs and add tests

commit.message:
fix(optim): keep a parameter's checkpointing strategy across an update (#5618)

* fix(optim): keep a parameter's checkpointing strategy across an update

The module optimizer takes a parameter off the tape to update it and
lifts the result back with `Tensor::from_inner`, which assigns the
default gradient-checkpointing strategy. A model trained under balanced
checkpointing therefore came out of its first optimizer step with every
updated parameter on the default strategy while its inputs and any
frozen parameter kept the balanced one, and the next forward refused to
merge the two. Training with gradient checkpointing could not get past
its first step. L-BFGS lifts its parameters back the same way when it
unflattens them and had the same problem.

Both now lift through `from_inner_with_strategy`, which restores the
strategy the parameter carried before the update. A test steps a model
on a device with balanced checkpointing, checks the updated weight's
strategy against the device's, and steps it again.

* refactor(optim): capture and restore a parameter's context around an update

Review feedback on #5618: `from_inner_with_strategy` was a public function for
what is an optimizer-internal reconstruction, and the checkpointing strategy was
one of three pieces of parameter state the mapper carried across the update by
hand.

`ParameterContext` is crate-internal and holds all three. `capture` takes the
gradient-retention flag, the distributed flag and the checkpointing strategy off
the parameter before it leaves the tape; `restore` lifts the updated value back
and puts them on. The module optimizer's mapper loses its three local bindings
and their cfg, and L-BFGS restores the same context instead of forcing
`require_grad` on every parameter it writes back — a parameter that was frozen
now stays frozen through a step.

fix(optim): keep a parameter's checkpointing strategy across an update (#5618)

* fix(optim): keep a parameter's checkpointing strategy across an update

The module optimizer takes a parameter off the tape to update it and
lifts the result back with `Tensor::from_inner`, which assigns the
default gradient-checkpointing strategy. A model trained under balanced
checkpointing therefore came out of its first optimizer step with every
updated parameter on the default strategy while its inputs and any
frozen parameter kept the balanced one, and the next forward refused to
merge the two. Training with gradient checkpointing could not get past
its first step. L-BFGS lifts its parameters back the same way when it
unflattens them and had the same problem.

Both now lift through `from_inner_with_strategy`, which restores the
strategy the parameter carried before the update. A test steps a model
on a device with balanced checkpointing, checks the updated weight's
strategy against the device's, and steps it again.

* refactor(optim): capture and restore a parameter's context around an update

Review feedback on #5618: `from_inner_with_strategy` was a public function for
what is an optimizer-internal reconstruction, and the checkpointing strategy was
one of three pieces of parameter state the mapper carried across the update by
hand.

`ParameterContext` is crate-internal and holds all three. `capture` takes the
gradient-retention flag, the distributed flag and the checkpointing strategy off
the parameter before it leaves the tape; `restore` lifts the updated value back
and puts them on. The module optimizer's mapper loses its three local bindings
and their cfg, and L-BFGS restores the same context instead of forcing
`require_grad` on every parameter it writes back — a parameter that was frozen
now stays frozen through a step.

feat(tensor): validate matmul rank in TensorCheck (#5580)

Tensor::matmul is defined generically over Tensor<D, K>, so rank-1 inputs
compile but have no matrix dimensions. TensorCheck::matmul short-circuits
for D < 2, letting invalid calls reach the backend, where they fail in
inconsistent ways: ndarray panics with "attempt to subtract with overflow"
(ndims - 2 underflows), tch returns a 0-dim dot product, and cubecl has no
valid kernel input.

Reject ranks < 2 in TensorCheck with a clear error, mirroring the tri()
check, and add a regression test.

feat(tensor): apply TensorCheck to remainder, powi, powf, hypot, atan2 (#5564)

* feat(tensor): apply TensorCheck to remainder, powi, powf, hypot, atan2

Element-wise binary ops like add, sub, mul, and div already check device
and broadcast compatibility via binary_ops_ew, but remainder, powi,
powf, hypot, and atan2 went straight to the backend without that check.
A device or broadcast mismatch therefore fell through to
backend-specific panics instead of a consistent Tensor Operation Error.

Add check!(TensorCheck::binary_ops_ew(...)) to those five ops, matching
the existing pattern, and cover each with a regression test that asserts
the Tensor Operation Error (verified to fail if the check is removed).

Ref: #5562

feat(tensor): add assert_shape! and debug_assert_shape! macros (#5554)

* feat(tensor): add unpack_shape!, assert_shape! and debug_assert_shape! macros

Shape assertions for module boundaries. A bracketed pattern has one slot per
axis: a bare name binds the axis size (unpack_shape! only), `=expr` and integer
literals check it, `_` skips it. The pattern length is bound to `[usize; N]`
from `Tensor::dims()`, so a rank mismatch is a compile error. Axis checks are
always-on in unpack_shape! and assert_shape!; debug_assert_shape! compiles out
without debug assertions, like debug_assert!.

The macros live in burn-derive, are re-exported from burn-tensor and the
prelude, and are documented in a new Forward Contract section of the book.

Inspired by the burn-contracts crate by Crutcher Dunnavant.

* refactor(nn): use shape macros for boundary checks in burn-nn and examples

Replace hand-written dims comparisons in the cross entropy, cosine embedding,
CTC and RNNT losses, positional encoding, multi-head attention and cross
attention with unpack_shape! and assert_shape!. Multi-head attention now
checks key and value against the query batch and d_model as documented.

The MNIST examples pin the input to [batch_size, 28, 28], which the hidden
size already assumed. The text examples check mask_pad, labels and targets
against the token batch and sequence length.

Box the Expr in the shape macro's Slot enum to silence large_enum_variant.

* refactor(nn): use debug_assert_shape! in module forward passes

Attention and positional encoding are hot paths, and the tensor operations
they call validate shapes in every build. Their boundary checks now compile
out in release; bindings go back to array destructuring. Loss checks stay
always-on since they run once per step.

Also list burn-derive as a dependency of the burn-tensor publish job, since
burn-tensor now depends on it.

* refactor(derive): echo the shape macro input verbatim in panic messages

Capture the macro input text before parsing and use it as the message
prefix, replacing the token re-spacing heuristics. Drop the dead rank-check
branch, the redundant trailing-token check, and the hand-built literal
expression. Multi-head attention reads the key dims inside the debug block
instead of in release. The book's macro guidance now states one criterion.

* feat(tensor): wrap shape macros in burn-tensor and make all module checks always-on

Public unpack_shape!, assert_shape! and debug_assert_shape! are now
macro_rules! wrappers in burn-tensor that forward $crate to hidden proc
macros, so the expansion calls Tensor::dims by path and a Shape argument is
a type error instead of a truncated check. Docs move onto the wrappers with
runnable examples, compile_fail cases and a should_panic doctest that
exercises the debug path in CI.

Attention and positional encoding go back to always-on checks: a size-1
axis broadcasts through the following operation, so a debug-only check left
release builds unprotected. Tests cover the new panics, trailing commas,
single evaluation, hygiene and release gating. A compound expression without
`=` now gets a hint, the MNIST examples name the image size, and the book
guidance makes assert_shape! the default.

* refactor(tensor): remove unpack_shape!, name axes with let [..] = dims()

With a compile-time rank, unpack_shape! without checks is a synonym for
`let [b, t, _] = x.dims()`, and with checks it did two jobs in one macro.
The two remaining macros only check: assert_shape! and debug_assert_shape!.
A bare identifier in a pattern is a compile error pointing at `=name` or the
array pattern. Call sites in burn-nn and the examples name axes with the
array pattern and check with assert_shape!; the book and tests follow.

* refactor(tensor): drop the `=` sigil from shape macro slots

With no binding macro left, every slot is a check, so the sigil that told a
check apart from a binding has nothing to disambiguate. A slot is now any
usize expression or `_`, and `assert_shape!(mask, [batch_size, seq_length])`
reads like the `# Shapes` doc line. The bare-identifier error and the
missing-sigil hint go away with it.

* docs(tensor): show expression slots in the shape macro docs and book

Examples now cover names from dims(), arithmetic on names and on literals,
a config field, and the wildcard, so a reader sees that a slot is any usize
expression.

* feat(tensor): add a `..` rest slot to the shape macros

A pattern may contain one `..` standing for any number of axes, so
`assert_shape!(input, [.., d_model])` works in a method generic over
`const D: usize`. Slots after `..` index from the end. Exact patterns keep
the compile-time rank check; a pattern with `..` checks a runtime minimum.
The feed-forward block, layer norm and RMS norm now check their last axis.

* refactor(nn): use `..` shape checks in rank-generic modules

Group, instance, batch and local response norm, rotary encoding and Linear
check the axes their docs promise with one assert_shape! each. Group norm,
batch norm, local response norm and rotary encoding replace hand-written
rank or channel checks; instance norm and Linear gain the check their
`# Shapes` section already stated. Batch norm and rotary encoding now also
check the channel and d_model axes.

* docs(tensor): show the channels-first rest pattern

* fix(nn): read parameter shapes without materializing, document panics, add tests

Feed-forward, RMS norm and batch norm read the parameter shape through
Param::shape() instead of val(), which under a reparameterization such as
LoRA ran a matmul just to learn a dimension. ShapeInput now captures its
own echoed call text while parsing, removing the token-skip assumption in
the entry points. Attention, cross attention and CTC document their panics,
the debug_assert_shape! docs state that a `..` rank check is runtime only,
and tests cover suffix slots before a wildcard, prefix mismatches with `..`,
the debug path with `..`, and the remaining untested burn-nn checks.
